title: Insider buys with the SEC filing attached. Free MCP server, no key.
author: Tradestar_Insider
selftext:
Form 4 buys, 13D, 13F, 8-K. Every row links to its filing. No filing, no row.

New: transaction date, acceptance time, 10b5-1 flag, 4/A link on every buy.

Ask it to verify a claim. It answers confirmed, partial or not found, with the link.

No scores. No sign-up. Endpoint in the first comment.

comments.author: filwu
comments.body:
Does each row, including a 4/A correction, also expose when that version first became queryable through your API? The [README](https://github.com/TradestarV5/insider-signals) says ingestion runs once per weekday and new filings surface the next business day.

For a hypothetical filing accepted at 20:10 UTC but first served at 07:00 UTC the next day, a backtest simulating information obtained through this API should wait until 07:00. The SEC record could have been public earlier. Keeping SEC acceptance time and first service availability separately would let users model that delay; a last-synced timestamp wouldn't recover the latter. I haven't tested the endpoint, so I'm asking whether that history is already retained.

replies.author: Tradestar_Insider
replies.body: Today each row carries the SEC acceptance stamp (acceptance\_datetime). It doesnt carry the time we first served it. So the delay you describe cant be recovered from the API yet. We will add it: first\_served\_at on every row, set once on first write and never changed. A 4/A correction is its own row and gets its own value. Rows served before the field existed will show null with a partial\_fields note. We dont backfill guesses.

replies.author: filwu
replies.body: One detail to pin down: does "first write" mean the transaction that makes the row queryable through the public endpoint, or an earlier ingestion write? In a hypothetical batch stored at 07:00 UTC but exposed at 07:05, a replay at 07:02 should still treat it as unavailable. If those are the same atomic step, first-write time covers that distinction. Otherwise, recording the publish boundary separately would avoid treating ingestion time as service availability.

replies.author: Tradestar_Insider
replies.body: Hm good distinction. We define first\_served\_at as the publish boundary: the first moment the public endpoint would have returned that row. Not the ingestion write. If the two are one atomic step in our pipeline, they coincide. If not, the stamp is set at exposure, not at the store write. In your example a replay at 07:02 gets nothing. The README will state which case applies.
